text:
Fathers house stood on a
hill.


A yellow hill against a. hot,
blue Sky-above the warm, blue
water of the bay. White gulls
dipping, weaving, drifting
through the sun drenched air.


Cleaning white clouds rolled
across the blue sky, casting
dark shadows on the bay, dark
stains as purple as the spilled
wine on the decks of the little,
dago. fishing boats. Lateen
sails on those boats copper
bright as they came scudding
home against the sunset fire.
The sound of songs coming
over the water. strange for
eign words that flowed smooth
as oil or broke into the sharp
staccato of castanets. High,
chattering songs. Low, sleepy
songs, as the boats lay tied to
the rickety wharves in the
evening, the water clucking,
lisping, between the piles. The
nights were never quite black
a powdery violet, with
flickering points of scarlet
where the braziers burned on
the freshly scrubbed decks.
Dark. shining faces with rings
in their ears, passing through
the glow of the flames,
laughing, singing, their white
teeth flashing. The smell of
frying fish. :. garlic. the sour
smell of wine. drifting with
the smoke


The town lay scattered be-
tween the bay and the hill. One
long main street-its ramshackle
wooden pavement on stills above
the deep, black winter mud.
above the deeper, golden sum.
n1er dust that smelled of grapes
and fish and eucalyptus gum.


Roads ..andered AimlessIy


From the main street, narrow,
rutted roads wandered aimlessly
in every direction-down to the
bay-back into the hills-over
the hills to the wide tule
marshes where the tidewater ran
in secret, silvery sloughs between
the peacock darkness of the
reeds. between the great
patches of ooze and slime that
were gold and crimson and
phosphorescent blue in the turn
ing light.


And always, along the narrow
streets, there drifted in another
silent tide, the smell of salty
mud, dried purple figs, violets,
pomegranates. fruity sunshine
=. slightly bitter fog.


Sunshine and fog-they were
not climate, they were Presences.

TALLAHASSEE, Fla, January e.
The Florida Supreme Court yesterday
quaShed permit to a motor truck line
paralleling the Seaboard Air Line Rail
way on the grounds that the railroad
was adequately serving the territory


The permit had been issued by the
State Railroad Commission to H. T.
Pace allowing him to operate a truck
line between here and Jacksonville.


The opinion gof the Supreme Court
reviewed the 1929 act of the Legislature,
which gave new powers to the Railroad
Commission, calling it General Pub
lie Utilities Commission vested with vast
powers affecting public welfare of the
entire State"


The court advanced the prediction
that if the Railroad Commission does
not look into the question of whether
the railroads are serving adequately
when motor truck lines apply for per-
mits, the time will come when all pas
Senger and freight, except heavy,
bulky, low grade, basic commodities" viii
pass from the railroads, which own
property and pay taxes, to motor lines
which operate over highways built and
maintained by the public for public
use"


The result of the commissions policy
In the Pace case, the opinion said,
would be ito bankrupt. or seriously
cripple rail lines, thus throwing thou
sands of railroad employees out of work,
impair efficiency of railroad service or
cause tremendous increase in freight
rates" while rapidly wearing out pub
lie highways, impeding ordinary use
OF roads and increasing the dangers of
life and limb. The court suggested the
law should be so construed that per-
mitS to truck lines would be granted
only where the public was not already
adequately served by established car
riers, whether rail or motor vehicles.

A 35-year old mother shot and killed

suicide at their home, in Eeesville, near
here. last night.


The deaG were:


Mrs. Russell Ward and her children.
Arlene, IL; Audrey, 8; Edith, Z, and
Richard, 4.


Authorities blamed financial troubles
for the tragedy. The mother. who had
told friends she was SO worried she
couldn't think" went to the village
school to get her children. She told
them they were going away"


The husband was in Wilmington at
the time of the shooting. He found
the bodies when he returned home.
Those of his daughters were on the bed
room floor. The mother lay in a door
way leading from the room and nearby
was the body of the boy.


Ward picked up the boy and found
he was not dead. He tried frantically
to revive the child. but death came
within few minutes.


The father toolmaker, had been
without employment recently, except for
odd jobs. He said his wife had been
acting strangely for several weeks and
had complained Of feeling i'll.


The house, a one-story cottage, was
dark but the doors were unlocked, when
Ward returned. He declared he went
first to the kitchen and. finding his
family gone, assumed they were visit
ing neighbors.


Several minutes passed before he
entered the bed room to find the bodies.
The mother left no note, but the coro-
ner was convinced she slew the children
and herself because she was tired of
poverty.


Ward, almost Frustrated by the trag-
edy said his wife often had threatened
to kill herself and the children. AS a
precaution he had taken the cartridges
from his revolver which he kept in the
bed room. The weapon was used ty
Mrs. Ward, however. and Ward was at
loss as to how she obtained cartridges.


Mrs. Ward apparently took the chill

KANSAS CITY, March 28.--Old man
Winter, who returned for his second
visit this month to the western fringe

today, but left his snowy mantle and an
icy breath.

sation of snowfall in the Dakotas, Ne

Texas and the Rocky Mountain States.

but one of several persons previously
reported missing in Nebraska had been
accounted for today The search con-
tinued for Boyd Edwards, years old,
vino had not returned from school to

apprehenSive over the effects of the
storm. While cattle losses in the Pan
handle section of Texas were not as

ports indicated severe damage to bud
ding trees.


Indications in Colorado and Mon
tana were that the storm had reached
its peak. Skies were clearing in Colo
RADIO and temperatures appeared to be
undertaking In Western Kansas many
persons reported missing were found
safe.


Trains into Kansas City from the
West and Southwest were from to II
hours late. Snow plowS were bucking
drifts from Phillipsburg, Kans., west
ward in an effort to clear the Rock
Island line between here and Denver.
Airplanes were grounded, wire COM
munications were only slightly affected.


Snow was scattered over the Pacific
Northwest and the mercury tlImbled In
Southern California. Fruit buds and
blossoms in apricot orchards in the
Yakima Valley of Washington and
citrus groves in the Imperial Valley,
California, were nipped. Some damage
was reported.


In most sections, however, orchard
lists and ranchers welcomed added pre-
cipitation.

SYRACUSE, October 13-Woman
students at Syracuse University, as they
begin the academic year, are facing a
thoroughgoing health program planned
by Mrs. Eugene Leonard, dean of
women, and her staff of assistants in
cooperation with the physical educa-
ton department and the health service
Of the university in q definite effort
to combat the present health hazards
among students. The program deals
with habits, activity and information.


Each girl will be scored on the basis
Of her health record. and the house
having the highest total scoring will
receive a silver cup in the Spring. The
girl with the highest score will have
her name engraved on the cup.


Scores to Be Kept


Scores will be kept in tennis, hockey,
hiking, basket ball. golf, bicycling, rid
ing. swimming, folk dancing. skating,
skiing. base bali. etc. Girls will be
credited for the number of times they
turn out and the spirit Of co-opera-
ton they show.


The section on health information
will be conducted through the medical
health service Of the university and the
living center having the highest per-
centage Of students at the three posi-
Die lectures Will receive The nlgn score
under this section. AS there are fifty
three living centers and three possible
lectures to each house, this will mean
q scheduling Of 159 lectures during the
year.


Seek to Cut Smoking


Every effort will be made. not so
much by discipline as by education and
persuasion, to lessen the number Of
occasional and habitual smokers.


Girls will receive plus scores for
healthful habits. such as drinking milk
and eating fresh fruit. and minus
credit for skipping meals and dieting
without doctors instructions. For
sleeping they will receive positive cred
its for being in bed before midnight
and for rest periods during the day,
and minus credits for all study and
recreation after midnight. Under
hygiene of the body they will receive
plus credits for drinking six glasses of
water daily, etc. Under miscellaneous
habits they will receive positive credits
for sun baths. regular study hours. and
minus credits for occasional smoking
and double minus credits for habitual
smoking between meals.

candy industry, which satisfies every
fourth sweet tooth in the United States,
hasn't heard about a business depres-
sion, orders and employment retaining
their normally through last year and
into this year.


Nineteen CONNECTION plants here pro-

Chicago became candy making

panies have intensified their bid for

ORANGE, Va, June 20.-President
Hoover and a small party, including
Undersecretary of the Treasury Mills,
arrived late tonight at the Chief Execu-
tive's Rapidan camp after an unevent-
full automobile trip from Washington.


Mr.. Mills, who has been closeted
much with the President during the
recent intensive conferences preceding
his announcement favoring a one-year
moratorium Of intergovernment debts,
rode to the camp with the President.


Leaving Washington at 8 o'clock, the
presidential party arrived at the camp
shortly after IL pm. Two of the Pres
ident's secretaries. Lawrence Richey
and Theodore Joslin, made the trip.


Mrs. Hoover. accompanied by their
son Allan and secret service men,
drove her own car much of the way
to the camp. A few other guests were
expected to join the party tomorrow.


The decision to come here for the
week end was made after the Presi-
dent virtually had abandoned plans for
the trip.

CHICAGO, February 23-Text books
have been traded for human experience
in the Northwestern University Law
School.


Dean Leon Green, in announcing a
new curriculum yesterday, said in re-
port to President Walter Dill Scott
that two years are enough to spend in
pursuit of text books and that hence
forth third and fourth year classes will
be shifted to the living laboratory of
Chicagoans and their everyday legal
problems.


After the student has learned how
the judicial process operates" Dean
Green said, "he will want to know
something more in detail about actual
problems which are troubling business,
how business men meet them, how
lawyers deal with them, how courts
deal with them"


Under the new curriculum, the third
and fourth year students will be in
troduced," the dean outlined, ITO the
intricate problems Of business organiza-
tons, financing, marketing, which in
turn includes banking, insurance, taxa
ton, arbitration and many sorts of spe-
cial contracts. Special problems and
actual cases related to one another will
be assigned to each student"


Students will be turned loose in the
court rooms, Dean Green said, to study
even the most trivial cases at close
hand.

ROACHDALE, Ind, December 10
Ten men armed with machine guns and
sawed-off shotguns blew open the safe
OF the Roachdale State Bank here early
this morning and escaped with $4,000
in cash and bonds. The bandits severed
telegraph and telephone cables and the
town was cut off from communication
with other places for some time.


Before entering the bank the men
kidnapped F. r. Jarvis, night telegraph
operator of the Baltimore g. Ohio Rail-
road, and locked him in the telephone
office above the bank with Pauline
Smith, 18. operator, and Pauline's sister,
aged 7, who was spending the night
with her


Cut Telephone Gables.


The robbers then broke into the
power plant and threw the switch, cut
ting current off from all of Roachdale
After cutting all telephone cables the
robbers broke into the bank and blew
the vault and fixtures to pieces with
three or four charges OF nitroglycerin
The entire front of the bank building
was blown out.


No one was able to give any informa-
ton as to how the bandits left town.
Jarvis said they walked about four
blocks and disappeared behind filling
station. That was the last seen OF
them.


Two men approached Jarvis as he
was taking mail from a Monon train.
They covered him with a gun and
escorted him to the town jail The
teleeraDher pleaded with them not to
lock him in and the men then took
him to the telephone Office.


Loss and Damage Insured.


The three were kept under guard
while the safe blowers worked. One
Of the robbers, authorities said, evil
IDENTIFY was an expert in the use OF ex-
plosiveS


The damage to the bank was est!.n-
ated at $1,000. Both robbery loss and
damage are covered by insurance.


Because of the wreckeu condition Of
the institution it was impossible to
conduct business today.

soon after daylight officers discovered
an automobile literally blown to bits.
Cylinders were split and separated and
pieces of the motor strewn about the
ground. On the larger sections of the
car powder marks were visible.


The machine carried Pennsylvania
license plate and yesterday afternoon
was reported by r. Goodman of 618
West Third street, Chester, Pa. as
stolen. The car was touring model.


County and State officers set to work
to solve the mystery, but today said
they were without clues relating to the
explosion. They said, however, they
were sure dynamite had been used.

By the Associated Press.


PORT OF SPAIN, Trinidad, Novem-
Der 24.-Two hundred convicts, lured on
by reports of ready work in Dutch
Guiana, escaped from a penal camp in
French Guiana, tramped miles through
swamps, crossed innumerable rivers and
endured great hardships only to find
they were the victims of a hoax.


There was no work for them. A
group of their fellow-convicts, to curry
favor with the authorities, had spread
the false rumors, so they might recap
ture some of the escaping prisoners.


The majority of the men returned
later to the forestry camp. TIL ring
leaders were punished by solitary con-
finement on the famous Devils Island
group of French Penal colonies.


Escape During Storm.


Reports had been circulated through
the camp that a railway line was being
constructed in the interior of Dutch
Guiana and that work was plentiful
The escape was made under cover of a
tropical storm


Lashing bamboo logs together, the
men crossed the turbulent Maroni River
FINALLY the Dutch frantier was reached
Into fever-laden swamps plunged the
men. sometimes Waging waist deep in
black, stagnant water. Through the
dense forest they struggled.


After days of privation and suffer-
ing they reached lonely village where
they discovered the employment story
was false. Weary and dispirited, some
OF the men surrendered to Dutch au-
thorlties. Others took the more direct
route OF marching back to the penal
camp.


Few Reach Freedom.


Escape from the French forestry
camps is comparatively easy, since the
men are employed on piece work. A
strong man may complete his DAYS
quota in five hours, leaving many idle
hours. The forest cantonements are
constructed OF light timbers and custody
OF the prisoners depends largely upon
the vigilance of a handful of gendarmes.
Offlclal figures indicate that about 200
men escape annually from the camps
but about so per cent surrender or are
recaptured. Only few reach freedom.
Most succumb to the fever swamps, the
snakes and wild animals that infest
the jungle.

SAN DIEGO, Calf, April 2c-The
death of comely 17-year-old Louise

slayer, who apparently strangled her

tree, puzzled police here today.


The body was found by picnic party

urday night and told them she was go

At the scene Of the tragedy police
gathered two slim clues One was the
double half-hitch knot which bound the
rope about the girls neck. The other
was an Army blanket found with the
girls clothes, her purse and q package
containing a pair Of hose she had pur-
chased Saturday.


The knot, police said apparently had
been tied by some one familiar with
handling rope. They suggested that IL
might have been tied by q sailor, or
one who had had sailors training. The
blanket was closely scrutinized for some
mark which might lead police to its
owner.


At the outset the case seemed as baf-
fling as that of the kidnapping and slay-
ing of 10-year-old Virginia Brooks, who
disappeared from her home here in Feb
ruary and whose body was found 5 miles
from the, city a month later. However,
police found no link which might con-
meet the crimes.


Father Aids Inquiry.
Miss Teuber's body had been stripped
of clothing. with the exception Of black
pumps and gun-metal hose. Investi-
| gators said there was every evidence
| that the girl had been dead before the
| long rope was thrown over the limb and
pulled to a stump 20 feet away TO be
| tied. The fact the body had not been
! lifted from the ground was significant,
/ they said. There were no bruises tndi-
| eating injuries which might have


caused death or unconsciousness.
| An autopsy was ordered to determine


whether Miss Teuber had been as
saulted.


Miss Teuber's father aided police in
questioning several suspects last night.
Sheriff's officers were studying a note
said to have been received today by
Teuber. All information regarding the


contents was refused by the officers, who
limited. however. the note had been
written by the girl, probably Saturday.

LONDON, June 9.-The admiralty
announced today that the British sub
marine, Poseidon. one of the largest in
the feet, had been sunk in a collision
near Weihaiwei, on the North shore
of the Shantung peninsula in China.


Five officers and twenty-six men were
saved, but two died after they were
rescued. Eighteen men are still miss
ing.


The submarine collided with a mer-
chant vessel. 81 miles north of Weihai-
wei early this afternoon.


The admiralty announcement said
vessels which had gone to the scene of
the collision included the Berwick,
Cumberland and Hermes.


The Poseidon was launched at Bar
row, England on June 81, 1929 She
was 260 feet long with 28-foot beam.


The accident is the second of its kind
within the past month.


A Russian submarine sank during
maneuvers in the Gulf of Finland. The
Soviet government has been reluctant to
discuss that accident, but other vessels
Of the fleet have been dragging the gulf
for the hull ever since the ship was
lost.

MOSCOW, July 14.-Eight Russian
army officers were killed yesterday in
an airplane accident near Alabino,
about 80 miles from here.


The victims were Assistant Chief
Triandafilow of army headquarters, AS
sistant Chief Kolenovsky of the mocha
nization department. a headquarters
officer, two senior officers, an observer
and two technicians.


The cause of the accident has not
been determined, but aviation authori-
ties believe the planes motor failed
and the ship crashed in forced land
ing.


People at Alabino said they had heard
the motor falter, then saw the plane
maneuvering as though seeking a land
ing place. There was a cleared space
which would have been large enough
for safe landing, but the plane over
shot 1t and crashed among the trees
of a dense woods. All the occupants
of the ship were killed instantly.

ST. JOHNS, Newfoundland, March
17.-An 18-year old girl last night car
ried on against tremendous difficulties
in an effort to send through static-filled
ether news of those who were aboard
the sealer Viking, which was destroyed
Sunday by an explosion.


Listed automatically on the records
of the Mackay Radio Co. as o. Bartlett,
the young woman, who serves as radio
operator on Horse Island, near which
the Viking was destroyed, spent feverish
hours tapping out messages for the
outer world, many of which were never
received.


Thought Movie Set.


Rumors of the explosion had reached
here earlier But it was known that
the Viking was chartered for motion
picture purposes and 1t was behetcd
what had been taken for disaster was
only a carefully staged scene. This be-
lief was shattered only when Miss Bart
let's message was read to Parliament
by the prime minister, and the govern
ments agencies marshaled and dis
patched to the Vikings survivors.


1t was at O'Clock Sunday night when
the girls first message flashed through
the air, giving the first actual hint of
the tragedy in the ice-filled waters
near the lonely island, which she shares
with three families.


Heard terrific explosion this morn
ing" she said "Wreckage of burning
steamer sighted about miles east Of
here. Also men travelling on ice toward
island"


Men on Ice Watched.


FTIoov, fOIIouyoJ apv{o,,c %
ing, while she watched the human
forms on the ice some miles away
While she watched she sent what little
news she could.


mo particulars at hand, yet" she
messaged. Ice in bad condition.
Heavy sea, wind blowing off shore.
First crowd of men may reach island.
Others have very little chance. Making
very slow progress"


Then came a disturbed note. The
three families who occupied the island
made hasty calculations and this
worried message came:


People have only sufficient sup
plies for selves. No medical assistance
here. No chance getting to mainland"


First Real News Obtained.


The night dragged, while on the
island the three families and the girl
made what precautions they could to
care for the mariners staggering to-
ward them through the Arctic cold
and against shrieking gale.


Meanwhile all the information at
Miss Bartlett's disposal had been sent
to Government officials. There wasn't
much. Simply that there had been an
explosion on an unidentified steamer
eight miles away. that the steamer was
in flames and that men we're walking
hn 20 ~


Early in the forenoon, however, came
the first sepcific news.


A trace of the girls excitement en-
tered the message, which began, THE
men have reached the island; in such
exhaustive condition could give no CO.
herent story. Impossible wire further
details now"


Name Of Vessel Learned.


Impossible, just then, perhaps, but
within a few moments she wired that
the ship was the viking; that the cap
tain was seriously injured and that the
cook, wireless operator and doctor were
missing.


The one man who could relieve her
and the man who could care for the
injured were missing. Nothing to be
done about it, SO, little later, she
passed on the word that dynamite, used
to free the ship when it became caught
in ice jams, had exploded in the ships
stern, demolishing the vessel aft and
setting her ablaze forward.


If Miss Bartlett was suffering from
fatigue or nervous strain from the
ordeal under which she labored, there
was no hint of it in the distressing
message that followed:


Men below and asleep when ex9lo-
sion occurred. Many blown to pieces
Twenty are dead and injured unknown"


And then the ether filled with static

ceived.

low prices for the year or longer, con-
struction gangs have laid mile after

plans which if carried out will make
this country spider web OF natural
gas lines.

Louis, Memphis. New Orleans, Atlanta.

Texas and the large Louisiana reserves.

Kentucky and Ohio. have diverted their

like Baltimore, and upper New YORK

nounced, indicate that cities along the

HAVANA, January 20.--Part Of Ha-

many homes we're flooded and residents
were terrorstricken because Of bomb
explosion which wrecked water main
at Llinas and San Carlos streets early
this morning.

neighborhood and brought sleepers from
their beds in fright. Water gushed from
the broken main, quickly flooded the
streets and poured into homes in the
neighborhood.


Property damage was considerable and
there was near panic, but no one was
reported injured.


Police were without a clue TO the
perpetrator of this newest of a series
of bombings and there was belief that
the bomb had been planted by the same
forces which have disturbed the city
in anti-government manifestations for
some time.

BY the Associated Press.


MADRID, October 5.-Victory for
most of their candidates in the interim
election to the National Assembly was
claimed today by Republican factions
allied with the provisional government.


Seventeen provinces voted yesterday
for % Deputies to fill vacancies created
when those winning several seats in
the last general election were required
to resign all but one. Returns are in
complete, but unofficial reports indi-
cate most of the contests were close.


The voting in Madrid, Barcelona,
Valencia and Seville, where there was
one vacancy each, was watched in
tently for signs of opposition to the
present regime. Early returns indicated
the Left wing candidate. Manuel Cos
sio, had defeated Jose Antonio Primo
de Rivero, son of the late dictator, who
campaigned from Madrid to vindicate
his fathers policies.


The election was without disorders
except for fist fights. There were few
arrests. Only about 40 per cent of the
electorate in the provinces involved
participated, as compared with 20 per
cent in the regular election.

More than 100000 women now are

a special Red Cross Committee was

NANTES, France, June 10.-Seven-
ty-seven victims Of the st. Phili-
bert steamboat disaster were buried to-
day after outdoor funeral services in
which thousands Of stolid Bretons par
ticipated.


They are stoios, these BretonS, prob.
ably the least emotional OF all the
French people, but many OF them wept
as the simple service marked the pass
ing Of more than 400 men, women and
children drowned in the Bay of Biscay
when the excursion steamer sank.


Aristide BRAND, who represents this
district In the Chamber Of Deputies,
marched from the Town Hall to the
ancient castle courtyard where the
services were held and stood up for
two hours until they were over. Then
his aides hurried him into an automo-
bile and back to his hotel for rest.


The city itself had suspended all buSi-
ness. Curtains were drawn, and flags
were at half-staf. Church bells tolled
and chanting choir boys preceded the
cortege from the castle courtyard to
the cemetery.

their money. The bandits were out
witted by the only woman passenger,
however. She was Ann Graham,
Columbus, who placed a diamond ring
in her mouth, dropped her purse to
the floor and kept her feet over it.
She saved both.


The passengers robbed and the
amounts taken included r. Scott Holley,

Roy T. Yates, 35-year-old financier

was so critically wounded today
he was unable to give police his
version of how he was shot.


Yates was found wounded yes
terday in the apartment of Miss
Ruth Jayne, an attractive blonde
of 27, who said she was the sena-
tors social secretary"


Paid Her Rent


Miss Jayne recalled little except
that a sustained drinking party
and quarrel over finances had
preceded the shooting.


Yates, married and the father
Of three children, was shot in the
abdomen. A revolver was found
beneath the window Of Miss
Jayne's apartment, but she said
she did not know where it came
from or who did the shooting.
She said she had known Yates
for four years and that he paid
her $112 monthly apartment rent
and gave her between $3.50 and
$500 every month.


Wife Visits Victim


Mrs. Yates visited her husband
at the hospital and remained
with him an hour. He was only
semi-conscious during her visit.

sit.

three parties sitting in the opposition
benches-Conservativ Liberals and
the new party. The Liberals usually
vote with the government. and Mosley's
followers probably will do likewise most

abandoned his seat among the Labor
ties and walked the few yards across
the historic hall to his new place there
were ironic cheers from the Labor
benches.


Lady Cynthia Mosley joined him a
few minutes later with several other
members Of the new party who will
vote with him in the critical division
on the unemployment insurance bill
which comes up for second reading
this afternoon.


The Governments position is some
what dangerous now, for both Mosley
and James Maxton. Labor left-winger.
have moved rejection of the measure,
and some Of the insurgent Liberals are
sure to vote against it.

BY the Associated Press.


CHARLOTTETOWN, P. E. T., De-
cember 15.-The Falconwood Hospital
for the Insane burned down early today
and three persons perished.


One was trapped by the flames. Two
others we're killed when they leaped
from windows.


Three hundred patients were driven
by the fire into the biting cold of the
night.


The origin of the fire has not been
determined. Flames were first seen
pouring from the upper section of the
west wing BY the time flremen ar
rived the entire wing was ablaze.


Blasting Proves Futile.


The water supply was inadequate.
Available pressure was not sufficient to
send stream into the burning build
ing. Dynamite was used to sever the
west from the east wing, but the SUP
ply of the explosive was too small and
the flames leaped the narrow gap and
soon were devouring the entire struc-
ture.


The property lost was estimated to be
between $250,000 and S500,000.


William McGuinn died in the flames.


John Mackenzie, trapped, jumped
from top window. He was killed in
stantly as his body struck the frozen
ground.


William Macdonald also jumped. He
died of injuries half an hour later.


The hospital staff succeeded in get
ting the other patients 20 safety only
with great difficulty. They were aided
by firemen. policemen and citizens Of
Falconwood drawn to the fire by the
sos painted in the skies by the mount
ing flames.


Officials Join Fight.


The mayor of Falconwood and the
city councillors adjourned session OF
council to Join the fire fighters. Pre-
mier Stewart also joined the rescuers,
and city physicians and clergymen were
other volunteer firemen and first aid
workers.


The patients, dazed, wandered uncer-
tainly about in the light of the fire, but
there was no disorder. Many patients
after the shock of their narrow escape
had passed, assisted in the work of
relief to those of their number who
had been injured or who faced suffer-
ing from the cold.


Bedding, clothing and hospital sup
plies were provided promptly by requi-
sition from other hospitals. the Jail, the
armory and stores. The patients were
taken to the infirmary and adjoining
buildings. Even stables were used, so
urgent was the need of getting the pa
tients out Of the cold.


Only few were injured and the OBJ
jective of doctors mainly was to fore
stall illness from exposure.


The west wing of the hospital was
built in 1878 the east wing in 1898.

LOS ANGELES. October % LP-
The strenuous police hunt for Winnie
Ruth Judd, wanted for the Phoenix
trunk murders. continued throughout
the West today. but the belief grew that
she either was hiding here or had COM
United suicide.


Although there were reports that per-
sons resembling the hunted woman had
been given rides by motorists near San
Diego and at Central California points
toward Sacramento. officers expressed
the belief she might not have left the
city.


The search was pressed while officers
prepared for an inquest over the bodies
OF the victims, Miss HedVig Samuelson
and Mrs. Agnes LIE Roi, which were
shipped here in trunks claimed by Mrs.
Judd.


Beaches and Hills Searched.
On the theory that Mrs. Judd's body
might be found in some out-of-the-way
place, police looked over the beaches
and hills around Los Angeles. Volun-
iteers peered into deserted cabins and
looked through the brushy underground
in canyons near the city.
Her husband, DR.. w. C. Judd. and
her brother, B. j. McKinnell, both ex-
pressed the belief that she would not
be found alive.


: Many friends of Mrs. Judd were in
terrogated. Guards were placed at
their homes in the hope the fugitive
would seek aid from acquaintance.


Oficers also endeavored to piece to-
gether a plausible motive for the STAY
ings of Mrs. Lc Roi and Hedvig Sam
.uelson, both of whom had been room
mates of Mrs. Judd and her close
friends


Insanity Is Suspected.


"All evidence shows it was a case of
insanity-but there was something that
caused the mind to perform such
CHASTITY crime" said Detective Inspector
D. A. Davidson. indications were
that jealousy furnished the background
for the slayings-but jealousy of what
is still undetermined"


Davidson sad Los Angeles police had
found no direct evidence of unusual
relations between the three women,
other than that they had been excep-
tionally friendly


That Mrs. Judd had been acting
irrationally for some time was disclosed
by her former employers, who said she
had acted "queerly" on numerous oc-
casions.


Davidson said police had wholly
abandoned the theory that Mrs Judd
had a man accomplice. The double
crime was committed Solely by the
woman, he said.


An inquest into the slayings is to
be held here tomorrow. The bodies
later Will be sent to Phoenix, where
another inquest is planned.

WICK, Scotland. February 21.-The
crew of the disabled Latvian steamer
Everline fought desperately tonight
against a wild gale from the southwest
that was driving their vessel toward
the rocky shores of the island of Yell,
in the Shetland group.
Early today the trawler Monimia Of
Wick got line aboard and started
TOWING the Everline to safety, but the
cable parted and the helpless drift be-
gan again.


A wireless message from the Latvian
ship tonight said she was going ashore,
but the captain of the Monimia thought
the vessel might just clear the rocks
If the wind held in the same direction.
He was unable to get new line over
because of high seas.
At last reports the Everline was five
miles north Of Essa Hess Light, drifting
northeast.

brother that OF naval lieutenant.


President Carmona, receiving them in

with the Order Of Avis and received
the Grand Cross of the Order of the
British Empire. Early tomorrow the
brothers will board the British cruiser
Kent for Bordeaux.

While her two smaller brothers and
sister were being carried to safety,
5-year-old Louise Gunnell, was burned
to death as she sought refuge under q
bed from flames which damaged the
Potomac Apartments, 1888 N street, this
morning


Her mother, Mrs. Anna Louise Gum
nell, was scorched about the face and
arms and her hair was singed as she
made frantic efforts to break through
the fire and reach the little girl.


The two-alarm fire broke out while
she was out of the apartment for O
minute. Returning, she discovered
smoke, coming through the wall and
found that her children had sprung the
latch of the door, locking her out Her
brother-in-law, Austin F. Gunnell, who
lives in the same apartment house.
broke in the door.


Fire Confined to Apartment.


The fire was confined to the Gunnell
apartment on the first floor, but smoke
filled the entire building, and several
persons were helped or carried to the
street by french. Residents of the
apartment house think the fire was
caused by defective furnace and say
the District fire marshal had been no.
titled several times Of the allegedly
dangerous condition.


Mary Rita Hurley, 5 years old, who
lives in the apartment next door to the
Gunnells, was carried from the apart
ment house by her 14-year-old brother
Jack after she had become frightened
when fireman attempted to help her.


Escorted From Building.


Lieut.. R. E. Oden, No Truck Com
pany, which was the first to arrive,
carried Raydell Kicks, years old, and
escorted her mother, Mrs. Mamie Kicks,
from the second floor. He also carried
June Woodbury., 9 years old, from the
third floor. None of the children or
Mrs. Kicks was injured.


The fire was discovered by Mrs. Gum
nell between 7:30 and 7:45 o'clock.
She had left her apartment to visit the
apartment on the same floor of her
brother in-law and his wife, Mrs. Ethel
Gunnell She returned q minute later
and observed smoke coming from the
wall separating her apartment from the
hallway.


Mother Finds Door Locked.


Attempting to enter. she found the
children had sprung the latch. She
rushed to her brother-in-law apart
ment with the news and Mrs. Ethel
Gunnell turned in the fire alarm. The
father of the children, Carl Gunnell. .
truck driver for the Standard Oil Co.,
had left home several hours earlier for
work.


Austin Gunnell broke in the door and,
with the two women, entered, in spite
of the flames, which had quickly spread.
Gunnell and his wife carried out Carl,
jr., years DID, and Rita, 2 years old,
while the mother of the children was
taking Robert, az months old, to the
hallway. There she put the baby on
the floor and went back into the apart
ment for Louise, who had hidden under
a bed. The mother could not find her.


Firemen arrived, and after the fire
was under control were able to reach
the child's body. The little girl was
taken to Georgetown University Hos
pital where DR.. L. j. Garcia pronounced
her dead. He said Louise may have
been asphyxiated by the smoke before
the flame reached her.


Second Alarm Sounded.


Acting Second Battalion Chief G. A.
Wells was in command of the first con-
tingent of flremen to arrive. He turned
in the second alarm, which brought
Chief Engineer George S. Watson to the
scene.


Upon entering the Gunnell apartment,
Chief Wells found a five-gallon can Of
auto radiator alcohol untouched by the
blaze He carried it out of harms way.


Austin Gunnell cut his hand break
ing in the door of the apartment


Mrs. Ethel Gunnel said after the
fire that she has complained to the
District fire marshalS Office several
times about the condition of the furnace.
Only last night, she said, coal gas it
gave off filled her apartment. The
apartment of Mr. and Mrs. Carl
Gunnell is directly over the furnace,
she said.


The father of the dead child was
notified of the tragedy by his sister
in-law. When he reached home he was
overcome and became hysterical.

city would have the world know, all
the shooting was just a noisome Incl
dent.


Commerce Increased.


While gangsterS slaughtered each

commerce and industry and spending
more than $3,000,000,000 since 1920 to

The towering skycrapers" of the
teens-the pride of their time-are
dwarfed today by peaks of masonry and
steel soaring so stories skyward. Scores

Amazing changes also have been
wrought in the outlying districts Dozens
of skyScraper hotels and apartments
tower above old homes and busting
business districts have appeared where
less than 20 years ago there was only
swampland and prairie.

A supreme artist, even in her adj
vancing years, Anna Pavlova has passed
away suddenly, just as she was about
to renew her active work in tour. She
was one of the great dancers Of all time.
For some years she had been compare
lively in retirement, making only occa-
sional appearances on the stage, showing
no diminution in her artistry, though
naturally somewhat less intense in her
performances than a decade ago. The
announcement Of her shockingly swift
illness and death brings wildly to mind
the thrill with which America wit
messed her superb performance twenty
years ago, when, after gaining fame in
Russia and winning recognition in other
European lands, she came to this coun-
try with her then dancing partner,
Mordkin. Hers was almost a new art,
though it comprised the elements of
the most ancient OF arts. Her vivid
personality, her marvellous grace, her
poetic expression in terms of movement
and rhythm made an instant appeal
and won the warmest plauditS. Her
success brought many into the field
who had less talent and whose per-
formances were less artistic. 1t re-
vived vogue for the classic interpre-
tive dance and undoubtedly abated the
trend toward vulgarity in the dance
that eventually, however, gained head
way and for a time prevailed. The
highest artistry fortunately remains
the ideal and Pavlova's contribution to
the worlds enjoyment has permanent
value that cannot be lessened by passing
lapses.

Before a single tree puts out a leaf
the woods are full of the first lush
greenery, and very good it looks to our
hungry eyes, if you can find child to
lead you to the SPOT where the onion
grass is sending frail green spears into
the pale green twilightS of earliest
Spring evenings. Now, wild onions are
not romantical we laugh when we hear
the very words, but the first green
leaves are the first green leaves, and
very glad we can be to see them, TOO.
Similarity, the skunk cabbage Is a
cause for Rabelaisian mirth, but there
is something bold and buccaneering
about its green, thick leaves, expand
ing under the leafless alders where the
golden taSse1S hang, and the ill-smell-
ing flower does not last long. The little
wood-leek, too, is blooming now in the
rich, sweet loans of the sleeps above
the Potomac. Unlike almost all our
neighborhood of Washington, its leaves
appear and die before its Towering stem
shoots up. Many plants bear their
flowers first and their leaves after
ward, but think of no other Wash
ington plants that drop their leaves be-
fore they flower, except the witchhazel.


Several times this Spring I have seen
women and children (all, / think, inn
migrants) cutting the big lush rosettes
of leaves of the Winter cress, itself an
immigrant waif from Europe. These
folks from the Old World, where every
rustic plant is known for its uses and
properties, know we'll that Winter cress
makes fine greens" The average
American countryman prefers a Starchy,
greasy diet of potatoes. corn, pork and
pie, but the most ignorant European
peasant makes the most of all the
wholesome green vegetables that grow
So carefully does he CLEAN from the
woods and fields that the amateur
plant lover has hard work to find much
to expend that love upon in q thickly
settled European countryside.


But do not, If you go hunting for
the first Spring greens" mistake either
the Winter-cress or the early dock
leaves for the beautiful false hellebore,
whose sulphurous green, great leaves,
rather like those of a ladys slipper,
but much bigger, are found at Laurel,
Hollywood Swamp, Lincolnton, Magno-
liza Run and Suitland Bog, for in this
weird plant of the lily family turks a
deadly poison.

HOLDENVILLE, Okla, July %
Standing waist deep in water and mud
of the receding rivers of Hughes County
as tom toms beat Indians are petition
ing the Great Spirit to send rain.


Prayers, unknown to the white man,
but voiced generations ago by the In
dams, are offered as the red men gather
several times each week on the banks
of the South Canadian and Little Rivers
to implore the Great Spirit for rain to
save their crops from drought.


The ancient colorful custom is being
witnessed for the first time in years.


The red men congregate in the dead
of night, coming in large groups from
farm houses and some from pretentious
homes The medicine man of the tribe
dressed in spectacular fashion, leads the
rites.


After campfires have been lighted
the men wade into the water and to
the muffled tom toms beat on the water
and pray in heir native tongue for
rain. Women and children line the
banks, keeping the fires blazing as the
ceremonies continue far into the night


When it rained recently for the first
time in several weeks, the Indians were
jubilant The tribesmen then increased
their efforts to bring more rain for crops
and gardens.

ICHANG, China, April "a battle
between a handful of American naval
guards aboard the Yangtze River
steamer Iping and a considerable body
of troops, supposedly Chinese Nationalist
soldiers. took place near here early
today. The Chinese soldiers opened fire
on the ship, but were silenced by the
American guns.


The Chinese poured sharp fire into
the Iping, which had been disabled by
striking rock in the Yangtze rapids
and was limping into Ichang for re-
pairs. The engagement was severe but
short, the American fire proving too
effective for the Chinese to withstand.


The attack was made supposedly by
Chinese Nationalist soldiers stationed
above Ichang to prevent the entry of
Communists into this city.


Had Anticipated Search.


Having heard Chinese soldiers were
searching ships. approaching, 1chang,
the Iping'S captain slowed down the
ship, expecting a boarding party to
approach and look for Communists. In
stead, the ships officers said, the SOL
diers attacked the Iping without ex-
PLANTATION, forcing the American guards
to fire.


Leo Bradley, f1rst-class seaman, United
States Navy, was wounded in the leg
and two Chinese aboard the ship were
gravely wounded. The Iping managed
to escape down the river after the gun
fire from her decks had afforded an
opportunity.


Bradleys home is in Indianapolis.


Was Second Attack.


This was the second attack on the
Iping in "a hours. When As miles above
Ichang last night, large group Of
Communists laid down a barrage
against the steamer and the American
guards replied with accuracy, silencing
the attack


The Iping. property of the American
controlled Yangtze Rapids Steamship
Co., ran onto the rocks 20 miles below
Chungking last Friday and was re-
f1oated next day. The area in which

munists.

With limited credits available and gar

them back to normal again. Through
Federal farm loans, loans on veterans
adjusted service certificates and limited
private credits the farmers have been
able to stand on their feet.


The mild Winter and ample rainfall

speeding preparation of soil for the new

this year.


Alabama, unlike some of the other

through the fertile Tennessee Valley
and a large area in the West Central
section.


Through the Tennessee Valley, how

farmers were nearly destitute, as food

sun, and cotton produced brought much
lower prices than customary.

nearby stables. where horses were quar-

betting sheds, the judges stand and

destroyed.


A high wind famed the blaze, but 1t
blew the flames and sparks in the OPP
posite direction from the stables in
which horses we're quartered, and these
buildings did not become ignited.

Today those men are dead.
Some doubtless died in decent,
quiet beds. But others had no
chance to choose their spots.
They took their death just as
it came beside the pan that
held disputed gold across
the deck that held an extra
ace before some bar or
brothel, wet lip stiffening while
it grinned, hot eye glazing while
it glanced.


So, one by one they went.
Now they're all gone. No bull
lets whistle down the empty
street. No picks and shovelS
clang beside the creek. The
hands that shot and shoveled
are no more. But still their
record stands, in tortured stone.


A Story of Hate


This gaunt, gouged granite
these contorted crags-those
lodges crumbling over secret,
stagnant pools - hold all the
story of their greed and hate,
their frantic struggle and their
furious lust. The rocks they
shamed, shame them-now they
are dead.


And yet above those rocks,
their church still stands. They
built that church, between their
brawls and blasts to satisfy
some vague and haunting dream.
Their gold is scattered and their
flesh is dead BUT THE
DREAM LIVES ON.


They lived like beasts in pits
they dug with their own hands


But high above those pits.
set a church.


And always men dig pits
with their own hands!


But always, too, they make
q place to dream


OF peace and truth, and
kinder, cleaner ways


And always, though flesh
dies, THE DREAM LIVES ON.

IF ever you are up in the neighberhood OF


Plymouth, Mass, you'll note there large
granite boulder, guarded carefully from the
weather under neat canopy and from humans
by an iron fence. Except for the date 1920,
carved upon its upper surface, there is nothing
remarkable about this large stone; in fact,
there are thousands of them in this region,
many Of them much larger than this one so
carefully guarded against humans and the
elements But if you know what took place
here In 1920, perhaps you'll know the reason
for the rock.


It was here in Plymouth that the Pilgrims
landed from the tiny Mayhower 3f0 years ago.
Many weary week they sailed from Europe
and when at last they sighted the bleak New
England Coast. it was with feelings of thanks
that they landed to establish their settlement.
The beach about their landing place was strewn
with these large boulders and it Just happened
that this large stone was handiest for landing
purposes. Out they stepped from their small
boats on the granite over 800 years ago.


OF course, these hardy men and children, too,
thought but little about the historical signifi-
canoe of the event and they never gave q
thought to that old rock which served as q
stepping stone into the new world. They
promptly forgot all about that doorstep, for
they had other things to think about. Many
years later, however, it was taken from its
resting place and only in recent times have
historical societies taken care of it.


The iron fence which now surrounds the rock
was placed there in recent times Souvenir
hunters began to chip pieces from this famous
stone and the entire rock would have dis
appeared in short order but for the fence which
now guards it for pesterity.

nected with the situation in Germany.
although the dispatches from Berlin

HAGERSTOWN, Md, April City
police. called by the sheriff, entered the
Washington County Jail here yesterday
at dinner time and, with drawn guns,
forced half hundred menacing Fed
eral prisoners back into their cells,
quelling for the time being what might
have been a serious riot


A letter struggled out Of the Jail by
one of the prisoners told of the riot,
which was admitted today by Sheriff
w. Bruce Downin. The note promised
that If conditions complained of were
not remedied other riots would take
place. All of the men were locked in
their cells today.


Bedlam broke out in the jail shortly
after noon yesterday and when dinner
was served at 4 o'clock the prisoners
threw down their plates and assumed
menacing attitude. Sheriff Downin
acted promptly in summoning city pc
lice and the men were herded back into
their cells.


In his letter to a newspaper today,
the prisoner said the men had rioted be-
cause of poor and insufficient food and
the lack of proper sanitary conditions.
The prisoners stated if the conditions
were not corrected more serious riots
would take place


Forty-eight Federal prisoners are
quartered in the jail, most of them pro-
hibition law violators sent up from Bal
timore City because of crowded jail
conditions there. ~


Sheriff Downin said the Federal pris-
oners come to the jail here flushed with
money and expect unusual privileges,
such as being allowed to roam outside
OF the jail at night and visit movie
theatsrS and take automobile rides. He
SAID the prisoners informed him such
treatment was accorded them in other
Maryland jails.


The sheriff said he had allowed the
men many liberties, such as stoves on
which to cook their own food, radio sets,
and permission to roam freely about the
corridors He said the county was given
only rs cents per day to feed each pris-
oner, of which SIS cents went for food.


Grumblings and cat-calls greeted per-
sons who approached jail today.

Gen. Adolphus w. Greely, 88 years
old, erect, hale and hearty still after
half century, steps out of his ro-
mantle past to become again identified
with plans for Arctic exploration.


The news grips the imagination and
StirS the blood.


Fifty years ago Gen. Greely, then
lieutenant in the United States Army,
led party of "a other intrepid men
into the deSolate Arctic regions. Three
years later, after terrible privation and
hardship, Gen. Greely and six of his
party were taken aboard a rescue ship
at Cape Sabine. Eighteen of the party
had starved or frozen to death because
they could not notify civilization of
their plight when an expected relief
ship failed to reach them. Despite
their suffering the survivors continued
to make meteorological observations up
to 40 hours before their rescue. They
had taken from the British the far
thest north record, held for 300 years.


The ill-fated Greely expedition Of
188l-84 looms heroic, grim and stark
IN the annals OF early Arctic discov-
cries.


Now Gen. Greely is cooperating in
an advisory capacity with Capt. Flavel
M. Williams, who with 20 men will
sail in June to spend two years at
Fort Conger, Ellesmere Island, north
ernmost land on the globe, where the
Greely party Wntered


Significant of civilizations progress
during Gen. Greely's life span, Capt,
Williams expects to be in constant
communication with the United States
by radio, and hopes to fly in compara-
tive luxury over the ice fields across
which the Greely survivors dragged
their toll and hunger weakened bodies
toward their rescuers.


Modern ingenuity and science have
conquered the poles and unlocked
many OF the secrets of the Arctic and
Antarctic regions, but modern con-
quests fail to dim the glory of the
achievements and the sacrifices of the

BY the Associated Press.


CHICAGO, october 15.--An order to
''shoot to kill'. was issued by Police
Commissioner James p. Altman TO halt
theater bombings.


The bombers can't keep getting
away he said last night. I'VE expect
to kill few Of them IL they keep this
bombing up"


Altman acted in compliance with
Mayor Anton j. Cermak's insistence
that drastic measures be taken at
once.


Thirteen theaters have been bombed
over a period of two months during
which labor controversy has been
raging between the motion picture
Operators union and the hundred
theater owners who are members of the
Allied independent Motion Picture
TheaterS Association.


Four attempts to end the dispute
have failed. The theater owners have
refused to comply with the unions de-
mand that two operators per shift be
employed in each of the hundred out
lying houses scattered through Cook,
Dupage and Lake Counties. Owners
claimed the $500 to SITS per week sal
airy paid the extra operator represented
the difference between their operating
at profit or less.


Offer to Accept Cuts.


The union offered to accept salary
cuts to offset the owners loss, but the
association rejected this.


The first indication of trouble was
given August ?, when owners notified
Thomas E. Maloy, business agent of
the union. who was recently indicted
for conspiracy and graft, that they
would close their theaters August
unless he consented that they operate
with one projectionist a shift. Maloy
refused. The theaterS closed, and re-
manned dark until August %. when
100 operators. brought from New York
and other Eastern cities, were licensed
to operate here. During this licensing
Joseph Maloy. Thomas brother, was
ousted as head Of the Licensing Bureau.


Police guards were installed at each
theater, and injunctions were obtained
to prevent the local union operators
from picketing and canvaSsing. Mat
tiers appeared to be moving smoothly
until August %, when the Ray. Ridge
and Olympia Theaters were bombed.


Since then the imported operators
have said they were slugged and shot at
and stencil bombs have been set of in
many theaters-not always those in
volved in the controversy.


Owners Blame Union.


The twelfth bomb was exploded late
Monday at the Monroe Theater while
the show was in progress. The thir-
tenth was tossed yesterday morning at
the Easterly Theater.


When the bombings started. the Cwn-
ers blamed the union Maloy denied the
allegations and offered $4,000 reward
for capture of the bombers. He added
that the owners were having their own
theaters bombed to create sympathy.


Last night officials of the union offered
to post their unemployed members as
guards at theaters to help police guards
prevent further violence. They made
this proposition as police took James
Aducci and five others into custody for
questioning.

The plea of l25 900 women for peace

schedule.

the desert and stuck in mud.


Then she led Women's suffrage

transcontinental trail for suffrage. In

trip petition for more women in Con-

With showmen muttering
surly threats, a gang of 10 laborers
today began dismantling the
tents of the stranded 101 Ranch

More than a score of police
men under Capt. Michael Raedy
were at the show grounds to pre-
vent disorder and forced several
of the unpaid workers to remove
marlin spikes and clubs from
their pockets when the men
threatened to break from the
control which has preserved
peace during the two weeks the
show has been "broke" on the
grounds.


Clustered about the cook tent

prepared to resist any effort to
strike the tent, although they
had not physically resisted when
the 70 imported laborers took
down the big top" and prepared

violence against the laborers and
against Fred Olmstead. represen-
tative of the owners, who was in
charge. Olmstead moved about
the circus lot guarded always by
at least three policemen.


Egypt" Thompson, famous old
circus man, brought here from re"
tirement to superintend the NOV
ing, directed the efforts of the
unframed and polyglot crew hired
for the difficult task.


The gang of laborers arrived at
the circus lot almost at sunrise
this morning. They had been re-
cruited in Baltimore. Alexandria
and Washington. Immediately
upon their arrival, they went to
work.


Pleas Prove Vain


Circus employees mingled among
them and tried the same tactics
which on previous occasions had
sent labor gangs away from the
lot.


They explained to the workers
that they had been seven weeks
without pay and urged them not
to take the bread out of our
mouths"


But tOday's labOrers were Of diff.
ferent mettle than that shown by
former gangs. They held their
ground and went to work on the
main tent.


Seeing their attempts to per-
suade the workers to desist we're
futile, the regular employees re-
tired to the cook tent.

exchanged q few epithets, but
there were no encounters.


just before noon, members of

smoking and chewing tobacco to
the stranded employees, while

watermelons.

NEW HAVEN, February 26.-In spite

Spring.


DR.. Marvin A. Stevens, Yale's varsity

March g. according to weather condi-

opens.

undergraduate daily, which has ex-
pressed critical opinions on many mat
ters concerning athletics this year.


Accompanying the foot ball an
nouncement the News printed a critical
editorial which claimed that such
Spring foot ball work "defies not only
the sentiments Of many a foot ball
player but likewise not a few of Yale's
opponents"


The News pointed out that "justi-
fication cannot be maintained on the
grounds that Yale needs projections
against her foot ball rivals" since Dart
mouth, Princeton and Army have
dropped Spring practice.

into the Nations bus and truck trans
portation question and plans to submit
recommendations on its findings to the
next Congress.


Before the final report Is drafted,
however, the commission will have laid
before it recommendations Of the study
by its examiners on the basis OF evil
dence placed before them by organiza-
lions. railroads and persons during the
hearings The examiners study Will
nave to be adopted, rejected or changed
after arguments are submitted TO
the commission.


The commission now has authority
to regulate interstate bus and truck
transportation and railroads are not
permitted to engage In highway traf-
fic directly.


Sought Coordination.


Two years ago the commission, after
being told by railroads that the truck
and bus systems were making serious
inroads into their traffic, both freight
and passenger, initiated the proceeding
with view to trying to develop co-or-
dination between highway and railroad
transportation.


Under the direction of Commissioner
Brainard. Examiners Flynn and Stephan
held hearings in every section OF the
country. Railroad employees and eXecu-
tives, bus and truck operators, civic
organizations and State regulatory
bodies were heard.


At the close of the hearings here re-
Gently. all parties were given until June
] to file briefs.


During the last few days the National
Grange Association of Railway Labor
Executives, National Automobile Cham
Der of Commerce, the Railway Express
Agency, motor bus and truck organiza-
tons and many railroads sent briefs.


Opposed Regulation.


The National Grange, the bus and
truck organizations, the Automobile
Chamber of Commerce, and even one
or two railroads asked the commission
to recommend that there be no Federal
regulation of highway traffic. The Della
ware and Hudson Railroad varied some
what from the other lines in urging
the commission to recommend Congress
to remove restrictions on managerial
functions of the railroads.


The grange argued the farmers had
been paying heavy taxes to build the
highways and trucks had helped develop
farm markets. 1t was opposed to any
regulation designed to equalize compe-
tition with railroads.


The motor bus and truck organiZa
lions expressed fear that regulation
would lead to monopoly and argued rail-
roads should be barred from the high
ways


Railroad labor executives charged
that motor transportation employees had
poor working conditions and pay and
could not better either without regula-
ton and organization. The express
company urged regulation of rates and
railroads of interstate lines and grant,
ing permission to the railroads to enter
the field.

ANNAPOLIS, Md, April 17.-Gov.

County and citizens opposing the
measure, while George Weems Williams
receiver for the company, and other
officials asked for its approval.


Mr.. Williams stated positively that

If the exemption was not granted, and
said that it was asked not for the
benefit Of the holders of the cOmpany's
securities, but for the public. which
needed the transportation facilities.


In reply to a question of the Gov
ernor, Mr.. Williams said that he was
not sure that the company could con-
tinue operation even if the exemption
was granted, but that its chances would
be improved.


City and county officials pointed out
the increased burden of taxation that

NANKING, China. September 10
Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh ar
rived here today for a four-day stay,
but because the colonel was not sat
ished with the place officials had
picked for him to land. Markings re-
ception was somewhat delayed.


The flying vacationists arrived over
the city at 2:36 pm. q SO am. Eastern
standard time), and after circling sew
eral times over the flooded Yangtze
River. finally alighted on Lotus Lake,
Just outside Markings rambling city
wall.


Built Special Wharf.


City dignitaries, however, had ar
ranged for him to land on the water
front, where they had constructed a
special wharf to which his monoplane
was to be moored, and had several
platoons of soldiers and some refresh
mentS on hand.


The Lindberghs made the S00-mile
hight from Fukuoka, Japan, in about
712 hours.


Meanwhile the dignitaries, including
Foreign Minister Wang, Consul General
and Mrs. Peck and Gen. Hung of the
Aviation Bureau, waited on the wharf,
in the river. Shortly after o'clock
an army plane, which had escorted
the Lindberghs, few over and signaled
them that the Americans had landed
on Lotus Lake.


Floods Swell Lake.


Oficials struggled to shore from the
wharf in native boats to dry land,
where they took automobiles and rushed
70 the lake to welcome the couple.


Lindbergh apparently believed the
Yangtze was too rough to make a
safe landing and, after five times cir
cling around and feinting at landing,
came down on the lake, which nor
mally is only Chinese park with an
artificial pond. The recent floods, how
ever, had increased it's size.

text:
BY the Associated Press.


BARCELONA, September 5.-The
general strike Of syndicalists, which was
called off last night after sanguinary
clashes between strikers and police, was
resumed today.


Firing continued throughout the night
despite assurances of syndicalist leaders
that their men would go back to work
today. Four omnibuses which resumed
operation were overturned by the strik-
erS. The press blamed President Fran
sisco Macia for the conditions Of unrest.


The uprising has cost the lives Of at
least % persons and wounded scores
more.


President Marcia radiocast an appeal
to the people last night to forego their
revolutionary attitude, which he said
was endsngering Catalania's chances
for autonomy with the central govern
ment. Many believe his words were
powerful enough to halt the movement


The bloodieSt encounter Of the out
break occurred when body of strikers
barricadsd themselves in the syndicaliSt
headquarters and defied authorities.
Equipped with rifles, revolvers and plen-
ty of ammunition, they held their own
against the repeated assault Of police
and civil guards.


BOmbardment Threatened.


At the end of six hours they sur
rendered when police wheeled light
artillery into position and threatened
to lombard them. The casualty list
read three killed and five wounded and
the prisoners numbered more than d
score.


Women were conspicuous In other
skirmisheS. One of them was killed
and several wounded when they stormed
the cathedral and sniped at police from
the roof. Others stood on streets and
balconies and beseeched their men with
tears to come home.


Syndicalist strikers called off the
strike after the government had
marshaled an imposing array of force
and applied near martial law to the
disorders. They temporarily dropped
their demands that political prisoners
be freed and the civil governor resign.
but they gave no assurance against
further bloodshed.


Squads Patrol Streets.


The crackle of machine guns and the
sound of rifle fire was heard all day.
Strong police squads patrolled the prin-
cipal streets and buildings. Those who
refused to halt were shot down. All
traffic was at a standstill Most peo-
pie stayed indoors or moved out with
their hands above their heads to in
dictate their pacifism.


Many times non-combatants, includ-
ing women and children, were swept by
bullets as police and strikers battled.
Strikers dug trenches outside the city
and blocked incoming travel. Others
besieged the police station. the post
office and the City Hall. but were driven
off. Cries of up with the Soviets"
were frequently heard as authorities
slowly regained control of the city.

was discovered by a watchman at 4:45
o'clock yesterday morning.

company plant. The first occurred

It Is really not difficult to make
rolled sandwiches of various sorts. The
bread for them must be fairly fresh
and not crumbly-the tougher kinds of
bread are better than the crisper kinds.


Cut the bread in thin slices, remove
the crusts, and butter well to the
edges. Then spread the bread with
whatever filling you wish to use-jelly,
chopped olives, finely minced nuts and
cream cheese, fish or meat paste Then
roll the sandwich-that is, roll the slice
of bread from one edge to the opposite
edge, pressing down the outside edge
firmly. The butter will make it stick
into position.


These sandwiches must be deity and
daintily made. After a little practice
they are not at all difficult, and they
are always tempting and attractive.
They may be made with both brown
and white bread for the sake of
variety.

BY the Associated Press,


HANKOW China, August 19-Flood
waters of the Yangtze River today broke
through the big Chiakow Dixie protect
ing Hankow's western suburb, inundat-
ing the native industrial district and
taking several hundred more lives.


Adding to the chaos of the last three
weeks, in which flood waters have
robbed some 10000, 900 persons of their
homes and left 10000 900 of them des-
titute, the renewed onslaught of the
river covered the highest ground in
Hankow under feet of water and the
lower areas 10 TO 20 feet under.


Epidemics More Serious.


Epidemics became more serious
among the refugees, who had nothing
to drink but flood water. Typhoid,
cholera and dysentery ragged unchecked
among the Chinese.


Industry in Hankow was demoralized.
Big -four. cotton and silk mills were
flooded when the dyke broke Such
confusion prevailed that it was impos-
sible to count the casualties


All foreigners were reported safe The
majority of foreign women had left or
were leaving on every available steamer.
Chinese were moving out by all other
disable channels Of travel Big river
junks were moving through what once
were streets, removing refugees and
valuables from homes and warehouses.


In Wuchang an important dixie burst
In the ancient city of Hanyang the
waters topped the gates of the city wall.


American on Hand.


Today's catastrophe here was wit
messed by John Earl Baker. American
relief expert and adviser to the Chinese
railway ministry, who is heading a
party surveying the stricken area The
flooded district includes the river bot
toms OF four provinces, Anhwei Hupeh,
Human and Honan.


Baker described the flood as probably
China's most terrible disaster in the
present century"


The Chinese government has organ
lied an extensive relief agency and has
issued a nationwide appeal for help
Inquiries have been made of the
American Farm Board looking toward
possible purchase of surplus American
wheat on credit for use among the
refugees.


Higher Than Monday.


The Yangtze River touched a level of
SO feet inches here today, ! inch
higher than the previous record level
of Monday.


Late Monday and Tuesday the
Yangtze began to recede. Then came
fresh importing from the north
through the Han River which empties
into the Yangtze here. More disasater
followed. A big dixie on the right bank
Of the Yangtze AZ miles down stream
collapsed flooding wide farming area


Until the last rise the dikes on the
right bank had held fairly well, keeping
q considerable area dry. However, along
the left bank. especially above here,
the bottoms were submerged as far as
the eye could reach Villages were in
undated entirely. Refugees were every
where, clinging TO ruined bikes and
other embellishments.


Calamity extended its grip even to
the lower Slang River, especially along
its left bank between Yochow and it's
confluence with the Yangtze All VIII
lagos and arabic lands along this
stretch were destroyed The Slang
finally receded. its food water passing
into the Yangtze.


Refugees Pack Streams.


All down-river steamers from Han
koW we're packed with refugees today
They had abandoned hopes Of saving
anything from their homes Evacua-
ton of Japanese women and children
was almost completed A few Ameri-
can and European women and children
remained in this vicinity, going to
Summer resorts in the nearby noun
tainS


Virtually all of Hankow was without
power, light and ice. The telephone
system broke Gown. Live high-tension
wires trailed across the water-swept
streets.


Reports here indicated conditions in
Hanyang and Wuchang, which are old
walled cities with narrow streets and
poorly constructed brick and rubble
houses, were worse than in buildings in
Hankow, Buildings in the older cities
were eollapsing, entrapping occupants


Authoritative foreign sources asserted
that despite the menace of epiaemics,
Chinese authorities had done nothing
in the way Of sanitation. Persistent
rumors Of threatened Communist at
tacks heightened the terriers for the
three cities

liquidation, says the United Business
Service, the movement Of the general
indexes Of business is definitely side
wise, not downward. No appreciable
change from present levels Is antici-
pated during May, but each week
brings the extended trough OF depressed
business nearer the end. Additional
weakness in the price structure, a pos
sible drought, and further bank and
brokerage failures may defer recovery,
but it Is confidently expected that gen.
eral business will not decline below the
low levels already made. The United
Business Thermometer registers busi-
ness this week at 236 per cent below
normal. which is approximately the
same level as the beginning of April.

1T has taken six years to work it all out, but
finally Uncle Sam is ready to make the lot
of the North Carolina sweet potato grower
lot sweeter.


After season upon season Of poor crops,
broken stands, late maturities and other gener-
ally unsatisfactory conditions, many Of the
growers appealed to the Department Of Agri-
culture to find what was wrong with their
methods and conditions. The answer is an
average crop of $40 bushels per acre on the
expei imental paintings, as compared with the
general State average of 100 bushels per acre.
In addition, the new methods are easier and
the fertilizer used lot cheaper than under the
former and less productive system


The farmers had used fertilizer containing
nitrogen exclusively from mineral sources. This
was used in large quantities and was placed
beneath the soil in the rows in which the
young plants were to be set out The young
plants were damaged when the roots came in
contact with the fertilizer, which resulted in
both poor and late yields.


The department experts tried fertilizer with
the nitrogen from animal and vegetable sources.
Smaller quantities were used and these were
broadcast on the surface of the ground after
the plants had been set, far easier method
than the other. The result was fine crops, and
crops ready for market at the time when the
price was at the peak. The results augur well
for the future of the North Carolina growers.

Barclay, 20 years old, Of New York,

passenger airplane in which they were
riding took fire in mid-air and crashed
into forest near Kurudjevo yesterday

two British passengers, the Norwegian
consul general in Constantinople and
two pilots, one French and one
Turkish.


What caused the disaster was unas-
certainable tonight The plane which
belonged to the Compagnie 1nterna-
tionale de Navigati ton Aeruenne, left
Constantinople for Bucharest yester-
day morning with the five passengers
and two pilots


1t was reported to have been seen
blazing in mid-air near Kurudjevo, and
it now lies in a charred heap In the
thick forest, surrounded by blackened
trees. The occupants had no chance
to escape, it was believed.


The bodies, also charred and mutt
lated. were found entangled in the
Wreckage All papers and luggage OF
the passengers were completely burned,
making the task of identification very
difficult.


Bulgarian authorities have opened an
Inquiry into the disaster.

Mayr announces, number of Winter

running and jumping coasting and

procession" with music and song, will
be held on New Year eve.

dow q thirteen-year- boy in brand
new store clothes watched q King and
Queen, attended by men in respondent
uniforms get out Of big. shiny auto
mobiles and walk in to shake the
Presidents hand. Later the boy peeped

and the Queen sat down to dinner with

and one wishes him long and pleasant

which started early Saturday in West
ern Kansas and Oklahoma. centered
over Missouri last night aNd apparently
was moving north and east into the
drought-stricken corn areas of the Mid
west.

Bureau also recorded rain in Nebraska
and at several Kansas points.

Iowa, but rain was expected to reach
the corn lands there by today.

reported no unusual weather, but snow
seemed general over Colorado, reaching
depths in some places which make
traffic dangerous. The snowfall, which
began in Colorado Friday night, was the
first major precipitation in the State in
more than two and ne-half months.


Goodland, near the Colorado line, re-
ported the heaviest precipitation today
in Kansas, 80 inch.


A general snowfall was reported in
Wyoming and in Western Nebraska.


Transcontinental airmail schedules

Lagos, capital of British Nigeria, Is

Lagos has been called the Bombay

few feet above sea level. Before the

Was Harvest" for Insects.

While all Lagos has not been made
over, several streets in the old portion

story, SpotlesSly white modern buildings
now occupy sites of dilapidated huts;
a handsome government building over
looks broad tree-studded lawn on a

1925; schools and hospitals have been

ROME, March 3O.-The world grain

met to investigate special phases Of the
difficulties.


Practically all of the delegates who
attended the conference received APP
pointmentS on the special committees,
and it was said that these would con-

day.


Thus far the conference is hopelessly
conferences will have to be held before
anything like a solution can be achieved.
The European countries along the
Danube still maintain the necessity of
a preferential tariff system, which would
mean a virtual boycott against nom
European wheat. In retaliation, the
great wheat-growing countries Of the
world have threatened to revoke their
most-favored nation treaties If the pref
erential tariffs are put into effect.


All countries admit that there has
been an overproduction of wheat, but
each ercphatically declared that it win
not reduce its own acreage. On the con-
trary, some countries, particularly Rus
STA, announced that they would do
everything possible to increase produc-
ton.


Engelbert Dollfuss, Austrian minister
of agriculture, in speech at this morn
ing's session, opposed reducing wheat
production and advanced the opinion
that the surplus could be disposed Of
through international agreement.

LONDON, April @Throughout
Europe women are turning their eyes
from their hearth to the political arena,
some with hope, some with determi-
nation and a not inconsiderable number
with actual distaste


Even Asia has begun to open its
political gates to wives and mothers.
The House of Representatives in Toxic
has passed bill granting women equal
franchise rights with men in elections
for city, town and village autonomous
assemblies.


The women of England and Germany
nave secured a far flrmer position in
politics than most of their sisters in
neighboring lands.


Turkish Women Progress.


Turkish women, though only liberated
from their harems during the past
decade, are already on their way to
Parliament They made their political
debut this year when the Kemalist
Government granted them the munic-
ipal vote, and those who know Renal
believe it well within the realm of
possibility that during next November's
general elections he will give them the
full franchise and the right to sit In
Parliament


In England, where the women fought
militantly for the franchise. IA other
women have followed the American
born Lady Nancy Astor into the House
OF Commons, and one, Viscountess
Sybil Rhondda, who is a peer in her
own right, is battering, though so far
without success, at the door of the
House of Lords


Women constantly are taking a more
extensive part in German public life.
There are now 80 feminine deputies in
the Reichstag. % of them being either
Socialists or Communists.


Austria More Liberal.


In Austria women were barred from
politics and even the professions until
the collapse of the AuStro- Hungarian
monarchy, but from that date their cru
SADIE into the forbidden realms began.
Parliament and the City Council were
opened 10 austrian women when the
Social Democrats came into power In
1919


The women Of France and Belgium
have, in large part, looked at political
life with apathy and often open distaste.
In neither country can they vote for
Parliament, though in Belgium they
can cast their ballots in communal
elections.
1lliteracy is woman's great stumbling
block on the road to politics in Greece.
Women neither can vote in parlimen-
tary elections nor sit in Parliament, but
in 1929 limited suffrage was given
women in municipal elections. This
vote was given women more than 30
years old who can read and write.


In Spain women can neither vote
nor hold elective Office. and the move
ment Tor women's suffrage Is so far
practically negligible.


Italian women, like their husbands.
are finding that the only road to po-
nucal influence winds through the
Fascist party.

Square Garden. Risko rallied in the
closing rounds, but could not overcome
the long lead piled up by his young
opponent in the early stages.

HaSSe,. so, who attended the bout as

of the three officials was not unani-
nous. The two judges named Poreda,
but Referee Kid Mcfarland picked
the veteran Risko.

the Cleveland battler back on his heels,

baker boy for the first five rounds. He
Jared the veteran repeatedly with
long left and crossed wicked rights to
the head and body. Risko had much
difficulty connecting with a looping
right, his principal weapon.
